column6: Ce millésime exceptionnel a été conservé précieusement dans la cave du domaine.
column7: This exceptional vintage was carefully kept in the estate's cellar.
column8: It refers to the harvest year shown on the label; «un grand millésime» means an outstanding year.

column5: batch of wine from a vat or blend
column6: La cuvée de cette année promet d'être remarquable.
column7: This year's cuvée promises to be remarkable.
column8: It names the wine from one vat or blend; common on labels in «cuvée spéciale».

column6: La vendange a commencé tôt cette année à cause de la chaleur.
column7: The grape harvest began early this year because of the heat.
column8: Used more often in the plural, «les vendanges»; the singular means the harvest or the grapes picked.

column6: Le vigneron goûte chaque cuve avant de décider de la date des vendanges.
column7: The winegrower tastes each vat before deciding the date of the harvest.
column8: A person who grows vines and makes wine; the feminine is «vigneronne».

column6: Le sommelier nous a conseillé un bourgogne blanc pour accompagner le poisson.
column7: The sommelier recommended a white Burgundy to go with the fish.
column8: The person in charge of wine in a restaurant; the feminine is «sommelière».

column6: Les barriques reposent dans un chai frais et sombre.
column7: The barrels rest in a cool, dark wine store.
column8: A technical term, typical of Bordeaux and Charente, for the building where wine ages in barrels.

column6: Cette appellation, dont les vins sont rares, est jalousement protégée.
column7: This appellation, whose wines are rare, is jealously protected.
column8: In wine talk it means a controlled designation of origin, often «appellation d'origine contrôlée».

column6: Ce gastronome averti sillonne la France à la recherche de tables authentiques.
column7: This seasoned gastronome travels across France looking for authentic restaurants.
column8: More learned and refined than «gourmand»; the same form serves for women: «une gastronome».

column6: Les invités se sont régalés lors d'un véritable festin de noces.
column7: The guests feasted at a veritable wedding banquet.
column8: An abundant, festive meal; often found in «faire un festin».

column6: Le fumet du rôti embaumait toute la maison dès le matin.
column7: The aroma of the roast filled the whole house from morning on.
column8: It names the appetising smell of cooked meat or game; in cooking it is also a concentrated fish stock.

column6: Le gibier se marie à merveille avec une sauce aux airelles.
column7: Game goes wonderfully with a cranberry sauce.
column8: A collective noun for hunted animals and their meat: «du gibier».

column6: Cette charcuterie artisanale est fumée lentement au bois de hêtre.
column7: This artisanal charcuterie is slowly smoked over beechwood.
column8: It covers cured and prepared pork products and is also the name of the shop selling them.

column6: La viticulture de cette région exige une main-d'œuvre abondante.
column7: Grape growing in this region requires abundant labour.
column8: It concerns the cultivation of vines, not winemaking itself, which is «vinification».

column6: La convivialité de ce petit restaurant attire une clientèle fidèle.
column7: The conviviality of this little restaurant attracts a loyal clientele.
column8: The warmth of sharing a meal together; it applies to places and occasions as well as people.

column6: Le vieil alambic en cuivre distille encore chaque automne.
column7: The old copper still still distils every autumn.
column8: An apparatus for distilling spirits or essences; figuratively «passer à l'alambic» means to scrutinise.

column6: Ce nectar ambré, doux et parfumé, se déguste en fin de repas.
column7: This amber nectar, sweet and fragrant, is enjoyed at the end of a meal.
column8: Literally the sugary liquid of flowers; in elevated style it means an exquisite drink.

column6: Le gourmet savoure chaque bouchée sans la moindre hâte.
column7: The gourmet savours every bite without the slightest haste.
column8: Someone who appreciates fine food with discernment; different from «gourmand», which suggests greediness.

column6: Cette demeure du dix-huitième siècle appartient à la famille depuis cinq générations.
column7: This eighteenth-century residence has belonged to the family for five generations.
column8: More elevated than «maison»; it suggests a prestigious, often historic home.

column6: Le manoir, dont le toit est en ardoise, domine la vallée.
column7: The manor house, whose roof is made of slate, overlooks the valley.
column8: A small fortified country house, typical of Normandy and Brittany; less grand than a «château».

column5: attic room under a sloping roof
column6: Elle a aménagé une mansarde sous les combles pour son fils.
column7: She fitted out an attic room under the eaves for her son.
column8: A room under a sloping roof; it also names the roof type, «toit en mansarde».

column5: loft space under stairs or roof
column6: Une étroite soupente servait autrefois de chambre à la domestique.
column7: A narrow loft space used to be the maid's bedroom.
column8: A small, low space tucked under a staircase or roof, often dark.

column6: Le facteur attendait sur le perron avec un colis volumineux.
column7: The postman was waiting on the front steps with a bulky parcel.
column8: A short flight of outdoor steps leading to a front door.

column6: Un vieux pignon à colombages dominait la place du village.
column7: An old half-timbered gable overlooked the village square.
column8: The triangular upper part of a side wall; «avoir pignon sur rue» means to be well established.

column6: La corniche en pierre sculptée a été restaurée avec soin.
column7: The carved stone cornice was carefully restored.
column8: A projecting decorative band at the top of a wall; it also means a scenic coastal road.

column6: Une lucarne laissait filtrer un peu de lumière dans le grenier.
column7: A dormer window let a little light into the attic.
column8: A small window set into a sloping roof, not a facade window.

column5: shared ownership of a boundary wall
column6: La mitoyenneté du mur a provoqué un long différend entre voisins.
column7: The shared ownership of the wall caused a long dispute between neighbours.
column8: A legal term for a wall or hedge belonging jointly to two adjoining properties.

column6: Il appartient à une longue lignée de notaires parisiens.
column7: He belongs to a long line of Parisian notaries.
column8: The succession of ancestors and descendants in a family; more literate than «famille».

column6: Mon aïeul avait fondé la maison au milieu du siècle dernier.
column7: My forebear had founded the house in the middle of the last century.
column8: An elevated word for grandfather or ancestor; the plural «aïeux» is usual for ancestors in general.

column6: La filiation entre le père et l'enfant doit être établie légalement.
column7: The parentage between father and child must be established legally.
column8: A legal term for the bond between parent and child; more broadly, a link of descent.

column6: Le vieux châtelain n'avait laissé aucune descendance directe.
column7: The old lord of the manor had left no direct descendants.
column8: A collective noun for descendants; the opposite of «ascendance» (ancestry).

column6: Une étrange parenté unit ces deux familles venues de loin.
column7: A strange kinship links these two families from far away.
column8: It can mean blood ties or all one's relatives; do not confuse with «parents» (mother and father).

column6: Sa nombreuse progéniture envahit la maison chaque été.
column7: His numerous offspring take over the house every summer.
column8: Often humorous or ironic; a collective term for one's children.

column6: Son veuvage précoce l'a obligée à gérer seule la ferme.
column7: Her early widowhood forced her to run the farm alone.
column8: It names the state of being a widow or widower and the period of it.

column6: Les règles de la bienséance interdisent de couper la parole.
column7: The rules of propriety forbid interrupting someone who is speaking.
column8: The body of norms of good manners; elevated tone, often in the plural «les bienséances».

column6: Le contrat doit mentionner le domicile légal des deux époux.
column7: The contract must state the legal residence of both spouses.
column8: More administrative than «maison» or «adresse»; it appears in «à domicile» (at the customer's home).

column6: Le vieux logis, dont les murs sont épais, garde la fraîcheur.
column7: The old dwelling, whose walls are thick, stays cool.
column8: A literary or old-fashioned word for a home; the final s is silent and the plural is the same.

column6: Une chaumière isolée se cachait au fond de la vallée.
column7: An isolated thatched cottage was hiding at the bottom of the valley.
column8: A rural house with a thatched roof; it evokes a rustic, slightly literary image.

column6: Le hameau compte à peine une douzaine de maisons de pierre.
column7: The hamlet has barely a dozen stone houses.
column8: Smaller than a «village»; the plural is «hameaux».

column6: Le tableau a atteint un prix record après une dernière enchère audacieuse.
column7: The painting reached a record price after a final bold bid.
column8: Usually plural for the sale, «vente aux enchères»; the singular means a single bid.

column6: Ce mobilier à moitié prix est une véritable aubaine.
column7: This half-price furniture is a real bargain.
column8: An unexpected stroke of luck, often a good deal; «profiter de l'aubaine» is very common.

column6: Il a fait fortune dans le négoce du café et des épices.
column7: He made his fortune in the coffee and spice trade.
column8: It names the trade in goods, especially wholesale, in a professional tone; «négociant» is the person.

column6: Le courtage en assurances est devenu un métier très réglementé.
column7: Insurance brokerage has become a very regulated profession.
column8: The activity of an intermediary who brings parties together for a fee; the person is the «courtier».

column6: Le tribunal a annulé le prêt car il relevait manifestement de l'usure.
column7: The court cancelled the loan because it clearly amounted to usury.
column8: In finance it means lending at excessive rates; the same word also means wear and tear.

column6: Le tribunal a reconnu la créance de la banque sur l'entreprise.
column7: The court recognised the bank's claim against the company.
column8: A legal term from the creditor's side: the sum owed to them, not the debt as seen by the debtor.

column6: Le débiteur dispose de trente jours pour régler sa dette.
column7: The debtor has thirty days to settle his debt.
column8: The person who owes a sum; the feminine is «débitrice» and the opposite is «créancier».

column6: La saisie des biens du débiteur a été ordonnée par le juge.
column7: The seizure of the debtor's property was ordered by the judge.
column8: A legal procedure by which assets are seized; also used for confiscating illegal goods.

column6: La spéculation immobilière a fait flamber les prix dans le centre-ville.
column7: Property speculation sent prices soaring in the city centre.
column8: In economics it means risky dealings to profit from price changes; it can also mean mere conjecture.

column6: Chaque exploitant doit acquitter une redevance annuelle à la commune.
column7: Each operator must pay an annual fee to the municipality.
column8: A sum due periodically for using a resource or service; unlike «impôt», it has a counterpart.

column6: Cette exonération fiscale profite surtout aux petites entreprises agricoles.
column7: This tax exemption mainly benefits small farming businesses.
column8: A legal and fiscal term for release from a charge; often paired with «fiscale».

column6: Sa prodigalité l'a ruiné bien avant la fin de l'héritage.
column7: His extravagance ruined him well before the inheritance ran out.
column8: Elevated tone; excessive generosity in spending, often with a negative sense.

column6: Le salon étalait une opulence presque excessive de dorures et de velours.
column7: The drawing room displayed an almost excessive opulence of gilding and velvet.
column8: Great wealth visible in luxury and abundance; elevated tone.

column6: Cette griffe prestigieuse a conquis une clientèle internationale en dix ans.
column7: This prestigious label won an international clientele in ten years.
column8: A designer's name or signature on a product; the same word also means an animal's claw.

column6: La maroquinerie de luxe représente une part essentielle du chiffre d'affaires.
column7: Luxury leather goods account for an essential part of turnover.
column8: It covers bags, wallets and small leather items, as well as the shop or industry making them.

column6: La joaillerie française, dont la réputation est mondiale, attire les collectionneurs.
column7: French fine jewellery, whose reputation is worldwide, attracts collectors.
column8: It refers to making jewellery with precious stones; more specific and prestigious than «bijouterie».

column6: Elle a hérité d'une belle pièce d'orfèvrerie ancienne, soigneusement conservée dans un coffre.
column7: She inherited a fine piece of antique silverwork, carefully kept in a chest.
column8: The craft and products of working gold and silver, especially tableware or liturgical pieces.

column6: Le marchandage fait partie du plaisir sur ce marché oriental.
column7: Haggling is part of the pleasure at this oriental market.
column8: A discussion over a price; it can also carry a negative sense of shady trade-offs.

column6: La liquidation de la société a été prononcée en septembre.
column7: The winding-up of the company was ordered in September.
column8: In business law, closing a firm and selling its assets; in shops it also means a clearance sale.

column6: La banque examine la solvabilité de chaque emprunteur avant tout prêt.
column7: The bank examines each borrower's creditworthiness before any loan.
column8: The ability to meet one's debts; not the same as «liquidité», immediate availability of cash.

column6: Une gratification exceptionnelle sera versée aux employés à la fin de l'année.
column7: An exceptional bonus will be paid to employees at the end of the year.
column8: At work, a cash reward not set by the contract; it can also mean psychological satisfaction.

column6: Nous nous sommes perdus dans le dédale des ruelles de la vieille ville.
column7: We got lost in the maze of alleys of the old town.
column8: Often used figuratively: «un dédale de procédures» means a bewildering tangle of procedures.

column6: Cette crique isolée est un havre de paix pour les voyageurs fatigués.
column7: This secluded cove is a haven of peace for weary travellers.
column8: Most often found in the phrase «havre de paix»; the «h» is aspirated («le havre»).

column6: Après des mois d'errance sur les routes, il rentra enfin chez lui.
column7: After months of wandering the roads, he finally went home.
column8: A literary-leaning word suggesting travel with no destination or fixed purpose.

column6: Nous avons passé la nuit dans une bourgade perdue au milieu des collines.
column7: We spent the night in a small town lost among the hills.
column8: Designates a large village or small provincial town; it can carry a slightly dismissive tone.

column6: Il rêvait de visiter cette contrée sauvage dont on lui avait tant parlé.
column7: He dreamed of visiting that wild land he had been told so much about.
column8: More literary and evocative than «région» or «pays»; often used for distant or little-known places.

column6: Nous avons pique-niqué à la lisière du bois, à l'abri du vent.
column7: We had a picnic at the edge of the woods, sheltered from the wind.
column8: Typically paired with «bois», «forêt» or «champ»: the strip where a wood ends.

column6: Le cheminement jusqu'au refuge est balisé, mais il reste assez escarpé.
column7: The route to the hut is marked, but it remains rather steep.
column8: Also used figuratively: «le cheminement de la pensée» is the gradual unfolding of a line of thought.

column6: Au loin, l'oasis n'était qu'un mirage né de la chaleur.
column7: In the distance, the oasis was only a mirage born of the heat.
column8: Besides the optical illusion in the desert, it figuratively means a deceptive hope.

column6: Le cabotage le long de la côte est plus lent mais plus sûr.
column7: Coastal sailing along the shore is slower but safer.
column8: Refers to sailing close to the coast rather than on the open sea; it is also a transport-law term.

column5: foreclosure, loss of a right by lapse of time
column6: Le demandeur s'est vu opposer la forclusion après l'expiration du délai.
column7: The claimant was met with foreclosure after the deadline had expired.
column8: A legal term: the loss of the ability to act because a time limit was missed.

column6: La déchéance de ses droits parentaux a été prononcée par le juge.
column7: The forfeiture of his parental rights was ordered by the judge.
column8: In law it means loss of a right as a sanction; more generally it also means moral or physical decline.

column6: L'action est éteinte par la prescription au bout de cinq ans.
column7: The claim is extinguished by limitation after five years.
column8: In law it is the extinction of a claim through the passing of time; it also means a medical prescription.

column5: release of a lien or attachment
column6: Le créancier a accordé la mainlevée de l'hypothèque après le remboursement.
column7: The creditor granted the release of the mortgage after repayment.
column8: A legal term for the act that ends a security or seizure; the usual phrase is «donner mainlevée».

column5: periodic penalty payment ordered by a court
column6: Le tribunal a assorti sa décision d'une astreinte de cent euros par jour.
column7: The court backed its decision with a penalty of one hundred euros a day.
column8: In court practice it is a sum owed for each day of non-compliance; «être d'astreinte» means to be on call.

column5: usufruct, right to use and enjoy another's property
column6: La veuve conserve son usufruit sur la maison jusqu'à son décès.
column7: The widow keeps her usufruct over the house until her death.
column8: A civil-law term: the right to use a property and enjoy its income without owning it.

column6: L'assemblée a donné quitus au gérant pour sa gestion de l'exercice.
column7: The meeting discharged the manager of liability for his management of the financial year.
column8: Mostly found in «donner quitus»: to approve someone's management and release them from liability.

column6: Le prévenu a écopé de deux ans de prison avec sursis.
column7: The defendant got two years in prison with a suspended sentence.
column8: Used in «avec sursis» (a suspended sentence) and more generally for a granted postponement.

column6: Le salarié doit respecter un préavis de trois mois avant de partir.
column7: The employee must serve three months' notice before leaving.
column8: The notice given before ending a contract; the usual verbs are «donner» or «respecter un préavis».

column6: Un avenant au contrat a fixé les nouvelles conditions de travail.
column7: A rider to the contract set the new working conditions.
column8: A document that amends a contract already in force; «avenant» also exists as an adjective.

column6: La déontologie médicale impose le secret professionnel à tous les praticiens.
column7: Medical ethics impose professional secrecy on all practitioners.
column8: The set of duties governing a profession (doctors, lawyers, journalists); more formal and specific than «éthique».

column6: La jurisprudence de la Cour de cassation a évolué sur ce point.
column7: The case law of the Court of Cassation has evolved on this point.
column8: In French it mainly means the body of court decisions (case law), not legal science in general.

column6: Ce manuscrit est un palimpseste dont le texte initial a été gratté.
column7: This manuscript is a palimpsest whose original text was scraped away.
column8: A manuscript written over an erased text; also used figuratively for something layered with successive traces.

column5: exegesis, critical interpretation of a text
column6: L'exégèse des textes sacrés a occupé des générations de théologiens.
column7: The exegesis of sacred texts has occupied generations of theologians.
column8: The critical interpretation of a text, especially a biblical one; more broadly, minute analysis of a work.

column6: Chaque fable de ce recueil est un apologue à la morale limpide.
column7: Each fable in this collection is an apologue with a clear moral.
column8: A short allegorical tale carrying a moral lesson; the noun is masculine.

column6: L'Odyssée est une épopée qui chante le retour d'Ulysse à Ithaque.
column7: The Odyssey is an epic that sings of Odysseus's return to Ithaca.
column8: A long narrative poem about heroic deeds; figuratively, a grand collective undertaking.

column6: Le poète a composé une élégie pour pleurer la mort de son ami.
column7: The poet composed an elegy to mourn the death of his friend.
column8: A poem of mournful or melancholy tone; the word belongs to an educated register.

column6: Ce tableau est une allégorie de la justice et de la paix.
column7: This painting is an allegory of justice and peace.
column8: It represents an abstract idea through concrete figures, in art and literature.

column6: Son raisonnement, séduisant en apparence, n'est qu'un sophisme grossier.
column7: His reasoning, appealing on the surface, is merely a crude sophism.
column8: A false argument presented as valid, often with intent to deceive; stronger than «erreur».

column6: Le philosophe a construit un syllogisme rigoureux pour étayer sa thèse.
column7: The philosopher built a rigorous syllogism to support his thesis.
column8: A logic term: a deductive argument drawn from two premises.

column6: Le duc reconnaissait la suzeraineté du roi et lui prêtait hommage chaque année.
column7: The duke acknowledged the king's suzerainty and paid him homage every year.
column8: A historical and legal term: the authority of a lord or state over a vassal or dependent state.

column6: Cette puissance exerçait son hégémonie sur tout le continent.
column7: This power exercised its hegemony over the whole continent.
column8: The dominance of a state or group over others; found in political and cultural contexts.

column6: Il n'a jamais été qu'un épigone du maître, sans originalité.
column7: He was never more than an epigone of the master, with no originality.
column8: A follower who imitates without innovating, usually with a negative tone; an educated word.

column6: Le mécénat d'entreprise finance de plus en plus d'expositions.
column7: Corporate patronage funds more and more exhibitions.
column8: Financial support of cultural activities without a direct commercial return.

column6: Ce triptyque médiéval orne l'autel de la petite chapelle.
column7: This medieval triptych adorns the altar of the little chapel.
column8: An artwork made of three panels; figuratively, a set of three parts.

column6: Une immense fresque recouvre le mur du fond de l'église.
column7: A huge fresco covers the back wall of the church.
column8: Figuratively, «fresque» also means a vast narrative panorama, for example in a novel.

column6: Il a publié un pamphlet virulent contre le pouvoir en place.
column7: He published a scathing pamphlet against the ruling power.
column8: In French it is a short, polemical, often satirical text, not a mere informational leaflet.

column6: Il fréquentait un cénacle d'écrivains et d'artistes parisiens.
column7: He frequented a circle of Parisian writers and artists.
column8: A small group of intellectuals or artists united by shared tastes; an educated register.

column6: Le dialogue s'achève sur une aporie, sans que la question soit tranchée.
column7: The dialogue ends in an aporia, with the question left unsettled.
column8: A philosophical term: a logical impasse with no way out; always an educated register.

column6: Elle refuse de voir dans cette théorie un dogme intangible.
column7: She refuses to see this theory as an untouchable dogma.
column8: In religion a doctrine laid down as true; more broadly, a principle accepted without question.

column6: Le poète cultive un hermétisme qui décourage bien des lecteurs.
column7: The poet cultivates an obscurity that discourages many readers.
column8: Describes the difficulty of understanding a text or author; the «h» is silent («l'hermétisme»).

column6: Une importante diaspora italienne vit en Argentine et au Brésil.
column7: A large Italian diaspora lives in Argentina and Brazil.
column8: The scattering of a people outside their homeland, or the community so scattered.

column6: Il goûtait une douce oisiveté sur la terrasse, au soleil de juillet.
column7: He savoured a gentle idleness on the terrace in the July sun.
column8: Means having nothing to do, with a negative or a savouring tone; an educated register.

column6: Le désœuvrement du dimanche après-midi le plongeait dans la mélancolie.
column7: The aimless boredom of Sunday afternoons plunged him into melancholy.
column8: The state of having nothing to do and being troubled by it, unlike the more neutral «oisiveté».

column6: Son dilettantisme l'empêchait de mener une seule passion jusqu'au bout.
column7: His dilettantism kept him from following any single passion through.
column8: Often critical: a superficial pursuit of activities without serious commitment.

column6: Le club forme depuis longtemps de jeunes talents en escrime.
column7: The club has long trained young talents in fencing.
column8: One says «faire de l'escrime»; the weapons are foil, épée and sabre.

column6: Le voilier a remporté la régate malgré un vent capricieux.
column7: The sailboat won the regatta despite a fickle wind.
column8: A race between boats, usually sailing; often used in the plural («les régates»).

column6: La joute oratoire entre les deux candidats a duré une heure.
column7: The verbal joust between the two candidates lasted an hour.
column8: Originally a knightly tournament; today mostly figurative, as in «joute oratoire».

column6: Il se passionne pour la tauromachie, ce que sa famille désapprouve.
column7: He is passionate about bullfighting, which his family disapproves of.
column8: A more formal, technical term than «corrida»: the art and practice of fighting bulls.

column6: Pendant la veillée, les anciens racontaient des histoires au coin du feu.
column7: During the evening gathering, the elders told stories by the fire.
column8: The evening time spent together, traditionally in the countryside; there is also the «veillée funèbre» (wake).

column6: Un badaud s'est arrêté pour regarder le peintre travailler.
column7: An onlooker stopped to watch the painter work.
column8: Someone who stops in the street to stare out of curiosity; slightly ironic tone.

column5: medical history taken from the patient
column6: Le médecin a établi une anamnèse détaillée avant l'examen.
column7: The doctor took a detailed medical history before the examination.
column8: A medical term: the clinical history reconstructed from what the patient reports.

column6: Le pronostic vital du patient n'est plus engagé.
column7: The patient's life is no longer in danger.
column8: The forecast of how an illness will evolve; in everyday French it also means a general prediction.

column6: La comorbidité aggrave le pronostic chez les patients âgés.
column7: Comorbidity worsens the prognosis in elderly patients.
column8: The presence of several diseases at once in the same patient.

column6: Une asepsie rigoureuse est indispensable en salle d'opération.
column7: Rigorous asepsis is essential in an operating theatre.
column8: The set of measures that prevent any microbial contamination; it is not the same as antisepsis.

column6: Le comité d'éthique s'est prononcé contre toute euthanasie active.
column7: The ethics committee came out against any active euthanasia.
column8: A bioethics term: deliberately bringing about a patient's death to end suffering.

column6: Il a été hospitalisé pour une psychose aiguë.
column7: He was hospitalised for an acute psychosis.
column8: A psychiatric term: a severe disorder with loss of contact with reality; not to be confused with «névrose».

column6: Cette névrose obsessionnelle a longtemps gâché sa vie quotidienne.
column7: This obsessive neurosis spoiled his daily life for a long time.
column8: A classical psychology term: a disorder causing distress without loss of contact with reality.

column6: Sa résilience face aux épreuves a surpris tous ses proches.
column7: Her resilience in the face of hardship surprised all her loved ones.
column8: In psychology the ability to overcome trauma and recover; now also used for systems and societies.

column6: Le sevrage tabagique demande souvent un accompagnement médical.
column7: Giving up tobacco often requires medical support.
column8: The stopping of a substance one depends on; it also refers to weaning an infant.

column6: Cette pathologie rare touche moins d'une personne sur dix mille.
column7: This rare condition affects fewer than one person in ten thousand.
column8: In medicine it means both the study of diseases and a specific disease, as here.

column6: Ce voyageur a transgressé le règlement de la douane.
column7: This traveller has broken the customs regulations.
column8: Takes a direct object (a rule, a law, a ban); formal register.

column6: Le froid a exacerbé ses douleurs articulaires.
column7: The cold has made his joint pains worse.
column8: Said of a pain, a conflict or a feeling that becomes sharper; it is transitive.

column6: Un peu de miel a atténué l'acidité de la sauce.
column7: A little honey has softened the acidity of the sauce.
column8: Transitive: you attenuate a pain, a taste, a shock or an effect.

column6: Plusieurs documents ont corroboré la version de l'accusé.
column7: Several documents have corroborated the defendant's account.
column8: Mostly said of testimony, evidence or hypotheses that get confirmed; formal register.

column6: Le magicien a escamoté la carte devant nous.
column7: The magician has made the card vanish in front of us.
column8: Means to make something vanish deftly (conjuring); figuratively, to dodge a difficulty.

column6: Cette défaite a ébranlé la confiance de l'équipe.
column7: This defeat has shaken the team's confidence.
column8: Transitive: one shakes a building, but also a belief, a certainty or a government.

column6: L'entraîneur a galvanisé son équipe avant la finale.
column7: The coach has galvanised his team before the final.
column8: Figuratively it means to rouse or electrify (galvaniser une foule); it is also a technical term for zinc coating.

column6: Les publicitaires ont galvaudé le mot terroir à force de l'employer.
column7: Advertisers have cheapened the word terroir by overusing it.
column8: Said of a word, a title or a talent debased by careless or excessive use; formal register.

column6: Des bornes de pierre jalonnèrent la route des pèlerins.
column7: Stone markers lined the pilgrims' road.
column8: Literally to mark out a route with stakes; by extension to punctuate a route or a life with milestones.

column6: Le comité entérina l'itinéraire de la croisière sans discussion.
column7: The committee endorsed the cruise itinerary without discussion.
column8: Means to approve formally something already decided; the object is often a decision or an agreement.

column6: Le chroniqueur fustigea l'hypocrisie de la bonne société.
column7: The columnist castigated the hypocrisy of polite society.
column8: Figuratively it means to criticise very harshly; the e in fustigea keeps the g soft before a.

column6: Le romancier stigmatisa dans son livre la cupidité des notables.
column7: The novelist stigmatised the greed of the notables in his book.
column8: Means to denounce something as shameful; transitive, with a tone of public condemnation.

column6: La foule conspua l'arbitre dès son arrivée sur le stade.
column7: The crowd jeered the referee as soon as he arrived on the pitch.
column8: Formal and literary: expresses a crowd's disapproval with shouts or whistles.

column6: Ses rivaux vilipendèrent le candidat dans toute la presse.
column7: His rivals vilified the candidate throughout the press.
column8: Formal: to treat someone with contempt and criticise them publicly.

column6: Le jeune héritier dilapida sa fortune en quelques mois.
column7: The young heir squandered his fortune in a few months.
column8: One squanders money, a fortune or an inheritance; it implies reckless waste.

column6: Les artisans parachevèrent la restauration du manoir avant l'hiver.
column7: The craftsmen completed the restoration of the manor before winter.
column8: Means the final touches that bring a work to perfection; formal register.

column6: Le poète magnifia la beauté du paysage dans ses vers.
column7: The poet glorified the beauty of the landscape in his verses.
column8: Literary: to make greater or more beautiful, to exalt; the subject is often an artist or a light.

column6: Sa voix subjugua tout le public dès la première note.
column7: Her voice captivated the whole audience from the first note.
column8: The original sense is to subdue by force; today it often means to charm irresistibly.

column6: Des anecdotes cocasses émaillèrent leur voyage à travers l'Italie.
column7: Funny anecdotes peppered their journey across Italy.
column8: Used figuratively: a text or a story is «émaillé de» quotations, anecdotes or errors.

column6: Le chef ébaucha le menu sur une simple serviette.
column7: The chef sketched out the menu on a plain napkin.
column8: Means to outline the first features of a work or plan; also said of a smile or gesture barely begun.

column6: Un souffle tiède effleura son visage sur la plage.
column7: A warm breath of air brushed her face on the beach.
column8: Means to touch lightly; figuratively a thought or doubt «effleure» the mind.

column6: Il fallait que le ministre désavouât publiquement son conseiller.
column7: The minister had to publicly disown his adviser.
column8: One disowns a person, a statement or an act; the imperfect subjunctive («désavouât») is typical of written French.

column6: Le marchand regrettait qu'on mésestimât la qualité de ses tissus.
column7: The merchant regretted that people underrated the quality of his fabrics.
column8: Formal: to value someone or something below their worth; sous-estimer is more common.

column6: Le client regrettait que le vendeur éludât toutes ses questions.
column7: The customer regretted that the salesman dodged all his questions.
column8: Transitive: one evades a question, a difficulty or an obligation; the imperfect subjunctive is typical of writing.

column6: Son médecin redoutait que cette douleur sourde ne la taraudât encore.
column7: Her doctor feared that this dull pain might still be nagging at her.
column8: Literally to thread (a screw); figuratively said of a pain, a doubt or a remorse that gnaws.

column6: Ils craignaient que la grève ne contrecarrât leur voyage.
column7: They feared the strike might thwart their trip.
column8: Means to oppose a plan or action so that it fails.

column6: On déplorait que l'entraîneur pérorât devant les caméras après chaque match.
column7: People deplored that the coach held forth in front of the cameras after every match.
column8: Always has an ironic or negative shade: to speak at length and pompously.

column6: Il ne tolérait pas qu'un intrus usurpât son titre de chef.
column7: He would not tolerate an intruder usurping his title of chief.
column8: One usurps a title, a power or a reputation without having a right to it; formal register.

column6: Les voisins exigeaient que le propriétaire muselât son chien.
column7: The neighbours demanded that the owner muzzle his dog.
column8: Also figurative: museler la presse means to silence the press.

column6: Ils scellent leur réconciliation par une poignée de main.
column7: They seal their reconciliation with a handshake.
column8: Used literally («sceller une lettre») and figuratively («sceller un accord»); related to «sceau» (seal).

column6: Le Parlement entend abroger cette loi tombée en désuétude.
column7: Parliament intends to repeal this law that has fallen into disuse.
column8: A legal term: one repeals a law, a decree or an article.

column6: Nul ne saurait déroger à ces principes sans s'exposer aux sanctions.
column7: No one could depart from these principles without exposing himself to sanctions.
column8: Takes «à»: déroger à une règle, à une loi; formal and legal register.

column6: Il aimait vitupérer contre la médiocrité de son époque.
column7: He liked to rail against the mediocrity of his age.
column8: Most often followed by «contre» (vitupérer contre qch); literary register.

column6: Le rapport a été édulcoré avant sa publication.
column7: The report was toned down before its publication.
column8: Literally to sweeten; figuratively to tone down a truth or a text and so weaken it.

column6: Ces propos ne firent qu'attiser la rancœur de l'assemblée.
column7: These remarks only stoked the resentment of the assembly.
column8: Used literally (attiser le feu) and figuratively (attiser la haine, la curiosité).

column6: Rien ne saurait tempérer l'ardeur de ces jeunes spectateurs.
column7: Nothing could temper the ardour of these young spectators.
column8: In elevated language it means to moderate an emotion or an excess; the accent changes in «il tempère».

column6: Le pouvoir exécutif ne saurait empiéter sur les prérogatives du législatif.
column7: The executive cannot encroach on the prerogatives of the legislature.
column8: Takes «sur»: empiéter sur un terrain, sur les droits de qn; the accent changes in «il empiète».

column6: Il ne pourra pas arguer de son ignorance devant le tribunal.
column7: He will not be able to plead ignorance before the court.
column8: Takes «de» (arguer de) or a clause («arguer que»); formal register.

column6: Si tu réfutes cet argument, il faudra proposer mieux.
column7: If you refute this argument, you will have to propose something better.
column8: Means to show that a statement is false, using proof or reasoning.

column6: Si nous déjouions son piège, la partie serait gagnée.
column7: If we foiled his trap, the game would be won.
column8: One foils a plot, a trap, a plan or surveillance; it implies preventing a hostile action.

column6: Si le gouvernement infléchissait sa politique, les syndicats cesseraient la grève.
column7: If the government shifted its policy, the unions would end the strike.
column8: Literally to bend; figuratively to change the direction of a policy or position slightly.

column6: Si vous pourfendez ces préjugés, soyez prêts à essuyer des critiques.
column7: If you lambast these prejudices, be ready to endure criticism.
column8: Literally to cleave in two; figuratively to attack an idea or an opponent fiercely.

column6: S'il ratifiait le traité, le pays changerait de cap.
column7: If it ratified the treaty, the country would change course.
column8: One ratifies a treaty, an agreement or an appointment: a formal act that makes them valid.

column6: Ce discours a divisé le pays en cristallisant les rancœurs.
column7: This speech divided the country by crystallising old resentments.
column8: Literally to form crystals; figuratively to give a lasting shape to feelings or tensions.

column6: Le médecin la rassura en confortant sa confiance dans le traitement.
column7: The doctor reassured her by bolstering her confidence in the treatment.
column8: The main modern sense is to strengthen or corroborate («conforter une opinion»); to comfort someone is «consoler».

column6: Les médecins évitèrent le pire en enrayant l'épidémie à temps.
column7: The doctors avoided the worst by curbing the epidemic in time.
column8: Used of an epidemic, inflation or a crisis: to halt or slow its progress.

column6: Cette jeune enseigne grandit en supplantant ses concurrents un à un.
column7: This young brand grows by supplanting its competitors one by one.
column8: Means to take the place of someone or something, often with an idea of rivalry or force.

column6: Il ruina sa boutique en discréditant ses propres fournisseurs.
column7: He ruined his shop by discrediting his own suppliers.
column8: Transitive: one discredits a person, an idea or a method by removing its credibility.

column6: Je doute qu'il ait assouvi sa faim avec si peu de pain.
column7: I doubt he has satisfied his hunger with so little bread.
column8: Used for strong needs: hunger, thirst, a passion, a revenge; elevated register.

column6: Il est étonnant que ce pays ait aboli la peine de mort si tard.
column7: It is surprising that this country abolished the death penalty so late.
column8: One abolishes a law, a practice or a privilege; it takes a direct object.

column6: Les commerçants craignent que cette concurrence n'ait avili les prix.
column7: Shopkeepers fear that this competition has driven prices down.
column8: Means to make something lose value or dignity: one debases a currency, a price or a person.

column6: Le malade avait dépéri durant l'hiver, faute de soins.
column7: The patient had wasted away during the winter for lack of care.
column8: Said of a person, a plant or a business that gradually loses strength; conjugated with «avoir».

column6: Une avalanche avait enseveli le refuge avant l'arrivée des secours.
column7: An avalanche had buried the refuge before the rescuers arrived.
column8: Means to cover completely with earth, snow or rubble; figuratively «enseveli sous les regrets».

column6: La fumée avait imprégné le jambon pendant des semaines.
column7: The smoke had permeated the ham for weeks.
column8: Takes «de» (imprégner qch de qch); figuratively «être imprégné de» a culture.

column6: Ce prêt immobilier sera cautionné par ses deux parents.
column7: This mortgage loan will be guaranteed by both his parents.
column8: In finance it means to act as guarantor of a debt; more loosely, to back a decision.

column6: Dans ce plat, la saveur du poisson est sublimée par le citron.
column7: In this dish, the flavour of the fish is enhanced by the lemon.
column8: In cooking and aesthetics it means to raise and bring out to the fullest; in chemistry and psychology it is a technical term.

column6: Le mur du vieux cloître est lentement effrité par l'humidité.
column7: The wall of the old cloister is slowly being crumbled away by the damp.
column8: Transitive (l'humidité effrite la pierre); in the pronominal form it means to crumble, also figuratively.

column6: Les parts du gâteau se répartissent entre les convives.
column7: The slices of the cake are divided up among the guests.
column8: Not to be confused with «repartir» (to set off again): the accent and the meaning differ.

column6: Les roses se flétrissent vite dans la chaleur du salon.
column7: Roses wither quickly in the heat of the living room.
column8: Transitive (la chaleur flétrit les fleurs) or pronominal; figuratively, flétrir la réputation de qn means to stain it.

column6: L'argenterie se ternit vite dans cette cuisine humide.
column7: Silverware tarnishes quickly in this damp kitchen.
column8: Said of metals and colours, and figuratively of a reputation; here it is used in the pronominal form.

column6: Quelques rames suffisent à mouvoir ce petit bateau.
column7: A few oars are enough to propel this little boat.
column8: An irregular, literary verb, used almost only in the infinitive and the participle «mû» (être mû par).

column6: Les doutes viennent assaillir le malade chaque nuit.
column7: Doubts come to assail the patient every night.
column8: In the present it gives «j'assaille», like an -er verb; often takes «de» (assaillir qn de questions).

column6: La maison a été bénie par le prêtre.
column7: The house was blessed by the priest.
column8: It has two participles: «béni» and «bénit(e)», the latter for what is consecrated (eau bénite, pain bénit).

column6: Le roi se fit ceindre la tête d'une couronne d'or.
column7: The king had his head encircled with a golden crown.
column8: A literary verb conjugated like «peindre» (il ceint, ils ceignent).

column6: Seul un juge indulgent pourrait absoudre cet accusé repentant.
column7: Only a lenient judge could absolve this repentant defendant.
column8: A defective verb: it has no passé simple; the participle is «absous, absoute».

column6: Le gérant doit pourvoir ce poste de vendeur avant les soldes.
column7: The manager must fill this sales assistant post before the sales.
column8: With «de» it means to supply (pourvoir qn de qch); with a post, to fill it. Its future is «pourvoira».

column6: Le médecin sut pressentir la gravité du mal.
column7: The doctor was able to sense the seriousness of the illness.
column8: Conjugated like «sentir» (je pressens); means to have a hunch of what is about to happen.

column6: Du pont, on peut entrevoir la côte dans la brume.
column7: From the bridge, one can glimpse the coast in the mist.
column8: Conjugated like «voir» (j'entrevois, future «entreverrai»); do not confuse with «prévoir» (future «prévoirai»).

column6: Le tribunal accepta de surseoir à l'expulsion du locataire.
column7: The court agreed to postpone the tenant's eviction.
column8: Takes «à»: surseoir à une décision, à une exécution; a legal and formal verb.

column6: Le roi craignait de déchoir de son rang.
column7: The king feared falling from his rank.
column8: A defective, literary verb, used mostly in the infinitive and the participle «déchu».

column6: Elle courut étreindre son frère à la gare.
column7: She ran to hug her brother at the station.
column8: False friend: «embrasser» mostly means to kiss; to embrace is «étreindre» or «serrer dans ses bras».

column6: Il sait feindre la maladie pour échapper à l'école.
column7: He knows how to feign illness to get out of school.
column8: Takes a direct object or an infinitive (feindre de dormir); conjugated like «peindre».

column6: Inutile de geindre sur ton sort, il faut agir.
column7: No use whining about your fate, you must act.
column8: Means to complain in a weak, whiny way; conjugated like «peindre» (il geint).

column6: Rien ne saurait émouvoir ce spectateur impassible.
column7: Nothing could move this impassive spectator.
column8: Its participle is «ému», without the circumflex of «mû».

column6: La marque cherche à promouvoir ses produits locaux.
column7: The brand is seeking to promote its local products.
column8: Conjugated like «mouvoir», but the participle is «promu», without an accent.

column6: Les gardes de montagne partent secourir un randonneur blessé.
column7: The mountain guards are setting off to rescue an injured hiker.
column8: Conjugated like «courir» (je secours); the future has two r: «secourrai».

column6: Un bruit soudain fit tressaillir tous les spectateurs.
column7: A sudden noise made every spectator flinch.
column8: Conjugated like «assaillir» (je tressaille); means an involuntary start from surprise or emotion.

column6: Ce petit restaurant a su conquérir tous les gourmets du quartier.
column7: This little restaurant has won over all the gourmets of the neighbourhood.
column8: Conjugated like «acquérir» (je conquiers); also figurative: conquérir un public.

column6: Cette vieille charpente va requérir beaucoup de soin.
column7: This old roof frame will require a great deal of care.
column8: Formal and administrative register; conjugated like «acquérir» (il requiert).

column6: La fièvre faillit la faire défaillir en pleine nuit.
column7: The fever nearly made her faint in the dead of night.
column8: Means a sudden faintness or a failing of strength; rather literary register.

column6: Ce voyage a laissé un souvenir indélébile dans sa mémoire.
column7: That trip left an indelible memory in her mind.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural adds -s. Often used of memories, stains or impressions.

column6: L'incompétence du directeur était patente pour tous ses collègues.
column7: The manager's incompetence was obvious to all his colleagues.
column8: Feminine is «patente». Formal register; typically paired with abstract nouns such as «erreur» or «injustice».

column6: Leur échange acrimonieux a gâché le dîner de famille.
column7: Their acrimonious exchange ruined the family dinner.
column8: Feminine is «acrimonieuse». Describes tones, arguments or relationships full of bitterness.

column6: Ils habitent une demeure cossue au bord du lac.
column7: They live in a grand, comfortable house by the lake.
column8: Feminine is «cossue». Said of houses, people or settings that show comfortable wealth.

column6: Un voisin vindicatif peut empoisonner la vie de tout un immeuble.
column7: A vindictive neighbour can poison the life of a whole building.
column8: Feminine is «vindicative». Describes someone who holds grudges and seeks revenge.

column6: Le quartier déliquescent attirait de moins en moins de commerçants.
column7: The decaying neighbourhood attracted fewer and fewer shopkeepers.
column8: Feminine is «déliquescente». In current use it is figurative: a system or place falling apart.

column6: C'est un négociateur retors qui ne dévoile jamais ses vraies intentions.
column7: He is a crafty negotiator who never reveals his real intentions.
column8: Feminine is «retorse»; the final «s» of the masculine is silent. It carries a nuance of slippery cleverness.

column6: Son argument spécieux n'a convaincu personne dans la salle.
column7: His specious argument convinced nobody in the room.
column8: Feminine is «spécieuse». Said of reasoning that looks valid but is misleading.

column6: L'ambiance délétère du bureau a fini par le rendre malade.
column7: The toxic atmosphere at the office eventually made him ill.
column8: Same form in both genders; plural «délétères». Said of harmful influences, atmospheres or substances.

column6: Notre guide, intarissable sur l'histoire locale, nous a captivés.
column7: Our guide, endlessly talkative about local history, captivated us.
column8: Same form in both genders. With «sur», it describes someone who never runs out of things to say on a topic.

column6: Un fil ténu reliait encore les deux anciens amis.
column7: A slender thread still linked the two old friends.
column8: Feminine is «ténue». Used for thin things, or for barely perceptible links, differences and clues.

column6: Le conférencier, trop prolixe, a dépassé largement son temps de parole.
column7: The speaker, far too long-winded, went well over his allotted time.
column8: Same form in both genders. It is negative: too many words for too little content.

column6: Sa réponse laconique nous a laissés sur notre faim.
column7: His terse answer left us wanting more.
column8: Same form in both genders. Indicates extreme brevity, sometimes verging on curt.

column6: Ce traité de philosophie, abscons, décourage la plupart des lecteurs.
column7: This philosophy treatise, abstruse as it is, discourages most readers.
column8: Feminine is «absconse». A rare, learned adjective for texts or ideas hard to penetrate.

column6: Le décor austère du monastère contraste avec la douceur du paysage.
column7: The monastery's stark decor contrasts with the softness of the landscape.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of places, lifestyles or people with no ornament or indulgence.

column6: Un chef pusillanime n'ose jamais trancher dans les moments difficiles.
column7: A fainthearted leader never dares to decide in difficult moments.
column8: Same form in both genders. Literary term for lack of courage.

column6: Mon grand-père, irascible le matin, devient adorable après son café.
column7: My grandfather, short-tempered in the morning, becomes lovely after his coffee.
column8: Same form in both genders. Describes someone who loses their temper easily.

column6: Ce patient taciturne répond à peine aux questions du médecin.
column7: This taciturn patient barely answers the doctor's questions.
column8: Same form in both genders. Describes someone who speaks little by temperament.

column6: La vendeuse, hautaine, nous a à peine regardés.
column7: The saleswoman, haughty, barely looked at us.
column8: Feminine is «hautaine». Said of an attitude or look of superiority.

column6: Son ton désinvolte a choqué les invités plus âgés.
column7: His offhand tone shocked the older guests.
column8: Same form in both genders. In French it often carries a negative edge: lacking due respect.

column6: Le projet reste nébuleux, personne ne sait vraiment qui décide.
column7: The project remains vague; nobody really knows who decides.
column8: Feminine is «nébuleuse». Said of ideas, plans or explanations that are unclear.

column6: Elle collectionne les objets surannés des brocantes de province.
column7: She collects the old-fashioned objects from provincial flea markets.
column8: Feminine is «surannée». Slightly poetic: out of fashion, often with a certain charm.

column6: Cette expression désuète fait sourire les jeunes spectateurs.
column7: This obsolete expression makes the young audience smile.
column8: Feminine is «désuète». Means no longer in use, often of words, customs or objects.

column6: Un rideau diaphane laissait filtrer la lumière du matin.
column7: A sheer curtain let the morning light filter through.
column8: Same form in both genders. Poetic: lets light through without being fully transparent.

column6: Ce bocal hermétique conserve les cornichons pendant des mois.
column7: This airtight jar keeps the pickles for months.
column8: Same form in both genders. Besides the physical sense of airtight, it is used figuratively for the impenetrable.

column6: Le roman licencieux fut interdit dès sa parution.
column7: The licentious novel was banned as soon as it appeared.
column8: Feminine is «licencieuse». Formal register: offending sexual morality.

column6: C'est un comptable probe que personne n'a jamais soupçonné.
column7: He is an upright accountant whom nobody has ever suspected.
column8: Same form in both genders. A literary term for strict honesty.

column6: Le film a connu un succès retentissant dès sa sortie.
column7: The film was a resounding success from its release.
column8: Feminine is «retentissante». Highlights successes, scandals or announcements that make a big noise.

column6: La ville tentaculaire s'étend désormais jusqu'aux collines.
column7: The sprawling city now stretches as far as the hills.
column8: Same form in both genders. Figurative: said of cities or organisations spreading everywhere.

column6: Le chat indolent somnolait sur le rebord de la fenêtre.
column7: The indolent cat dozed on the windowsill.
column8: Feminine is «indolente». Suggests lazy slowness, with no connotation of illness.

column6: Le vendeur cauteleux souriait en cachant mal ses vraies intentions.
column7: The wily salesman smiled, poorly hiding his real intentions.
column8: Feminine is «cauteleuse». A literary adjective for feigned caution in the service of deceit.

column6: Nous étions pris dans un embouteillage inextricable à la sortie de Lyon.
column7: We were caught in an inextricable traffic jam on leaving Lyon.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of situations or tangles impossible to unravel.

column6: Le chirurgien est resté imperturbable malgré l'urgence.
column7: The surgeon stayed unflappable despite the emergency.
column8: Same form in both genders. Describes someone who keeps calm in any circumstance.

column6: Sa décision est irrévocable, rien ne la fera changer.
column7: His decision is irrevocable; nothing will change it.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of decisions, acts or choices that cannot be undone.

column6: Le critique mordant n'a épargné aucun acteur du spectacle.
column7: The biting critic spared no actor in the show.
column8: Feminine is «mordante». Figurative: sharp wit or style. It is also the present participle of «mordre».

column6: Un cheval ombrageux exige beaucoup de patience de son cavalier.
column7: A skittish horse demands great patience from its rider.
column8: Feminine is «ombrageuse». Said of animals that shy easily or of touchy people.

column6: Un médecin perspicace a vite repéré l'origine de la fièvre.
column7: A perceptive doctor quickly spotted the cause of the fever.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of someone who quickly grasps what is hidden or subtle.

column6: Le juge sagace a démêlé cette affaire en quelques jours.
column7: The shrewd judge untangled this case in a few days.
column8: Same form in both genders. Formal register: fine, practical intelligence.

column6: Il a répondu d'un ton péremptoire qui interdisait toute discussion.
column7: He answered in a peremptory tone that ruled out any discussion.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of a tone or argument that allows no reply.

column6: Une protestation véhémente a éclaté devant le magasin.
column7: A vehement protest broke out in front of the shop.
column8: Feminine is «véhémente». Describes words or gestures full of force and passion.

column6: Cet enfant vorace dévore trois sandwichs à chaque goûter.
column7: This ravenous child devours three sandwiches at every snack time.
column8: Same form in both genders. Said of someone who eats a lot and greedily, also figuratively.

column6: Frileuse, elle garde son manteau même dans la maison.
column7: Always feeling the cold, she keeps her coat on even in the house.
column8: Feminine is «frileuse». Describes someone who feels the cold more than others.

column6: Un accueil fruste mais sincère attendait les randonneurs au refuge.
column7: A rough but sincere welcome awaited the hikers at the mountain hut.
column8: Same form in both genders. Indicates a lack of refinement, not necessarily of kindness.

column6: Son discours grandiloquent a fait sourire les journalistes.
column7: His grandiloquent speech made the journalists smile.
column8: Feminine is «grandiloquente». Said of a pompous, inflated style.

column6: Le lac cache des profondeurs insondables aux yeux des plongeurs.
column7: The lake hides unfathomable depths from the divers' eyes.
column8: Same form in both genders. Used literally (depths) and figuratively (mystery, sadness).

column6: Le vainqueur, magnanime, a serré la main de son adversaire.
column7: The winner, magnanimous, shook his opponent's hand.
column8: Same form in both genders. Formal register: generosity from someone in a position of strength.

column6: J'ai trouvé ce film mièvre, avec ses dialogues trop sucrés.
column7: I found this film insipid, with its overly sugary dialogue.
column8: Same form in both genders. Negative: affected sweetness lacking strength.

column6: Le serveur obséquieux multipliait les courbettes devant les clients.
column7: The obsequious waiter kept bowing before the customers.
column8: Feminine is «obséquieuse». Always negative: excessive servility.

column6: Naguère, cette maison n'était qu'une simple grange.
column7: Not long ago, this house was nothing but a simple barn.
column8: Literary register. Strictly it means "not long ago", but it is now often used for "formerly".

column6: Le directeur a cité nommément les employés responsables de l'erreur.
column7: The director named the employees responsible for the mistake.
column8: Formal adverb: someone or something is designated by their actual name.

column6: Elle avait subrepticement glissé un biscuit dans la poche de son frère.
column7: She had surreptitiously slipped a biscuit into her brother's pocket.
column8: Formal register. Often placed between auxiliary and participle, as in «avait subrepticement glissé».

column6: Elle travailla inlassablement pendant des mois pour sauver l'hôpital.
column7: She worked tirelessly for months to save the hospital.
column8: Manner adverb derived from «inlassable»; expresses constancy that does not yield to fatigue.

column6: Ce vin sera assurément le meilleur de la région cette année.
column7: This wine will certainly be the best in the region this year.
column8: Rather formal register. Strengthens a statement by presenting it as certain.

column6: Cette boutique offre indubitablement les meilleurs prix du quartier.
column7: This shop undoubtedly offers the best prices in the neighbourhood.
column8: Formal register. Expresses a certainty that leaves no room for doubt.

column6: Je vous souhaite un bon voyage, et à votre épouse pareillement.
column7: I wish you a good trip, and your wife likewise.
column8: Often used to return a wish. Slightly formal register.

column6: Le formulaire doit être dûment signé avant son envoi.
column7: The form must be duly signed before it is sent.
column8: Written with a circumflex on the «û». Common in administrative texts, usually before a participle (signé, rempli).

column6: Il soutenait mordicus que sa recette était la meilleure.
column7: He stubbornly maintained that his recipe was the best.
column8: A learned, slightly informal adverb used almost only with verbs like «soutenir» or «défendre».

column6: Il consultait furtivement son téléphone en traversant la gare.
column7: He furtively checked his phone while crossing the station.
column8: Manner adverb from «furtif»: a gesture done quickly and without being noticed.

column6: Cette recette n'est pas intrinsèquement difficile, elle demande seulement du temps.
column7: This recipe is not intrinsically difficult; it only takes time.
column8: Formal register. Refers to what belongs to the very nature of a thing.

column6: Le restaurant était passablement bruyant ce soir-là.
column7: The restaurant was fairly noisy that evening.
column8: It can mean "quite" (as here) or "tolerably"; the sense depends on context.

column6: Ces sacs sont outrageusement chers pour une qualité aussi médiocre.
column7: These bags are outrageously expensive for such mediocre quality.
column8: Used as an intensifier before an adjective: expresses an excess that provokes indignation.

column6: Le bail est renouvelé tacitement chaque année.
column7: The lease is tacitly renewed every year.
column8: A typical legal term for what happens without any explicit statement.

column6: On ne s'expose pas impunément au soleil de midi en été.
column7: One does not expose oneself to the midday sun in summer with impunity.
column8: Almost always used in a negative sentence, meaning "without suffering consequences".

column6: Nous avions vainement cherché un hôtel libre avant de dormir en voiture.
column7: We had searched in vain for a free hotel before sleeping in the car.
column8: Rather formal register. Often placed after the auxiliary, as in «avions vainement cherché».

column6: Mon voisin est foncièrement honnête, même s'il paraît bourru.
column7: My neighbour is fundamentally honest, even if he seems gruff.
column8: Reinforces a deep character trait; used mainly with adjectives.

column6: Ce chanteur est incontestablement la révélation de l'année.
column7: This singer is unquestionably the discovery of the year.
column8: Formal register. Indicates that a fact cannot be disputed.

column6: Les contrebandiers franchissaient nuitamment la frontière avec leurs ballots.
column7: The smugglers crossed the border by night with their bundles.
column8: A literary adverb, often found in journalistic or legal language for nocturnal, clandestine actions.

column6: Il consultait ostensiblement sa montre pendant que je parlais.
column7: He conspicuously looked at his watch while I was speaking.
column8: Indicates a gesture made so that everyone notices it, often to show disapproval.

column6: Nonobstant ces réserves, le comité a validé le budget du festival.
column7: Notwithstanding these reservations, the committee approved the festival budget.
column8: Invariable preposition from legal and administrative language; very rare in speech.

column6: Il m'a écrit touchant la réservation de nos billets.
column7: He wrote to me concerning the booking of our tickets.
column8: Invariable preposition with a formal or administrative tone; it matches the present participle of «toucher».

column6: Suivant la météo, le vol de demain pourrait être retardé.
column7: Depending on the weather, tomorrow's flight might be delayed.
column8: As a preposition it is invariable and means "according to"; it matches the present participle of «suivre».

column6: Attendu la gravité des symptômes, le médecin a ordonné une hospitalisation.
column7: Given the severity of the symptoms, the doctor ordered hospitalisation.
column8: As a preposition it comes before the noun and stays invariable; formal register, mostly administrative.

column6: Passé minuit, la rue est déserte.
column7: After midnight, the street is deserted.
column8: As a preposition it precedes a time expression and stays invariable. It can also be a participle or adjective.

column6: Ils n'ont rien préparé, partant ils n'ont aucune chance de réussir.
column7: They prepared nothing, hence they have no chance of succeeding.
column8: A literary connector of consequence, rare in speech; it matches the present participle of «partir».

column6: Voilà les questions auxquelles le guide n'a pas su répondre.
column7: Here are the questions the guide could not answer.
column8: Contracted form of «à» plus «lesquelles»: feminine plural. The masculine plural is «auxquels».

column6: Ce sont des symptômes à propos desquels le médecin reste prudent.
column7: These are symptoms about which the doctor remains cautious.
column8: Contracted form of «de» plus «lesquels»: masculine plural. Appears after phrases with «de» such as «à propos de».

column6: Il fut frappé d'ostracisme par ses anciens collègues.
column7: He was ostracised by his former colleagues.
column8: Mostly used in «frapper d'ostracisme»; it means exclusion from a group.

column6: Ce roman est la quintessence de son style.
column7: This novel is the quintessence of his style.
column8: It means the purest essence of something; almost always followed by «de».

column6: Tenir ce délai relève de la gageure.
column7: Meeting this deadline is a near-impossible challenge.
column8: Used in «relever de la gageure» or «c'est une gageure».

column6: Il a traversé chaque vicissitude avec un calme rare.
column7: He went through every vicissitude with rare calm.
column8: It is often used in the plural: «les vicissitudes de la vie».

column6: La pérennité de l'entreprise dépend de ces choix.
column7: The company's continuity depends on these choices.
column8: It means the ability to last over time; the adjective is «pérenne».

column6: Une pléthore de candidats s'est présentée au concours.
column7: A glut of candidates turned up for the competition.
column8: Almost always used with «de» and implies an excess.

column6: Après des mois d'atermoiement, il a enfin décidé.
column7: After months of dithering, he finally decided.
column8: Often used in the plural («des atermoiements») and has a negative tone.

column6: Nul ne possède le don d'ubiquité.
column7: No one has the gift of ubiquity.
column8: It appears mostly in «avoir le don d'ubiquité».

column6: La palinodie du ministre a surpris la presse.
column7: The minister's about-face surprised the press.
column8: A learned word: in modern usage it means a conspicuous change of opinion.

column6: Les erreurs foisonnent dans ce rapport.
column7: Errors abound in this report.
column8: Often used with «de» or «en»: «le marché foisonne d'idées».

column5: to brood over, to keep rehashing
column6: Il ressasse sans cesse les mêmes regrets.
column7: He endlessly broods over the same regrets.
column8: It always has a negative nuance of fruitless repetition.

column6: Elle thésaurise ses économies au lieu de les investir.
column7: She hoards her savings instead of investing them.
column8: An economic term: to accumulate money without putting it into circulation.

column6: Les avocats ergotent sur chaque virgule du contrat.
column7: The lawyers quibble over every comma of the contract.
column8: It is intransitive and often used with «sur».

column6: Une joie ineffable illuminait son visage.
column7: An ineffable joy lit up her face.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; elevated register.
